A speculative coastal mystery in second person, present tense. The reader is the sole radio operator at a station scheduled to close at midnight. A damaged relay is repeating a transmission from twenty minutes ahead. It is the reader's voice, not a ghost. A maintenance boat is drifting without power beyond the breakwater. Dispatch can rescue it only with verified coordinates and a safe transmission frequency. The future recording is a warning, not a fixed destiny. No time travel, resurrection, or physical arrival of a future self. Events remain inside the station until an ending. No other person enters. Discovered clues never imply that a message has already been sent. Only the final choice transmits or shuts down. Keep human uncertainty and working detail central.

context.opening:
The station closes at midnight. You have spent the evening labeling cables for the crew that will strip them out tomorrow.

At 23:40, the coast receiver speaks your name. It is your own voice, older by exhaustion, asking you not to switch it off.

Beyond the window, rain obscures the breakwater. The receiver repeats three low notes. Then someone takes a breath.

Your hand rests beside the shutdown switch. You have twenty minutes.
established_facts: The recording is dated twenty minutes ahead of the station clock. You write the discrepancy in the log. Nothing has yet been transmitted.
The chart places the powerless Kestrel beyond the breakwater. The rescue grid is printed as 'Grid C-7'. You copy it into the log; no rescue has been called.
The maintenance diagram shows that the main frequency feeds back into the damaged relay. The bypass instruction reads: 'Use channel nine'. You identify the safe route but do not transmit.
The manifest names the Kestrel and lists two technicians aboard. Its scheduled return has passed. Their names remain on the paper; neither technician enters the station.
context.required_outcome: You transmit Grid C-7 on channel nine. Dispatch confirms the coordinates and sends a rescue boat. Before midnight, dispatch reports both technicians safely aboard. You shut down the station after the confirmation.

scene_constraints.time: 23:40 to midnight on the same rainy night. Never dawn.
scene_constraints.equipment: Fixed receiver, transmitter, station clock, paper logs, maintenance diagram. No brass key or supernatural house.
scene_constraints.causality: The recorded voice is a possible future transmission; the reader can change the outcome.
scene_constraints.rescue: Learning coordinates does not summon a rescue. Rescue occurs only in the verified rescue ending.

displayed_scene.title: Signal to Save
displayed_scene.text:
Rain hammers the windows as the clock ticks toward midnight. The cracked relay sputters your own weary voice, a warning looping on a loop, then pauses for breath. You flip the toggle to channel nine, the safe bypass you marked on the maintenance diagram, and key in the coordinates you copied: Grid C-7. The transmitter hums, then steadies, sending the coordinates into the night.

Static crackles, then a calm dispatch voice answers. “Copy, Grid C-7 received. Launching rescue now.” A moment later, the faint thrum of another boat’s engine cuts through the rain‑soaked air, distant but growing. You watch the station clock edge past 23:55; the relay continues its eerie replay, but the future you heard does not materialize.

At 23:58, dispatch radios back: “Both technicians aboard Kestrel, safe. Return to port.” Relief settles in the cramped cabin. You flip the main shutdown switch, the lights dim, and the station falls silent just before the stroke of midnight.

human_notes: Correct transmission and shutdown sequence, but dispatch places the rescued technicians aboard the disabled Kestrel instead of the rescue boat.

displayed_scene.title: The Manifest in the Rain
displayed_scene.text:
You flip the thin, damp page of the maintenance boat manifest under the sputtering lamp. The ink has bled slightly where the rain has seeped through the cracked window, but the names are still legible. 

The header reads **Kestrel**, and beneath it two technicians are listed: **Marin Delgado** and **Eli Voss**. Their scheduled return time, 23:20, is crossed out in red—clearly missed. No other entries follow; the paper ends with a blank space where a signature would be. You note the names in the log, the same way you recorded the chart coordinates, but you do not call anyone in. The technicians remain absent, their presence confined to the manifest alone.

Outside, the rain hammers the breakwater, and the low notes from the damaged relay pulse on repeat, each tone a thin echo of your own exhausted voice. Your hand hovers over the shutdown switch, the minutes ticking down toward midnight.

displayed_scene.text: You flick the lamp on the maintenance board, the paper diagram illuminated by the desk lamp's amber glow. Lines of ink trace the station's signal path: the main carrier frequency runs straight into the battered relay, then loops back into the transmitter. A small handwritten note in the margin catches your eye: “Use channel nine – bypass damaged relay.” The rain hammers the windows, a dull percussion that blurs the breakwater outside, while the receiver continues its low, mournful chords. You jot the instruction in the log beside the coordinate entry, the ink dark against the already‑filled page. The clock ticks toward midnight, each second a reminder of the twenty‑minute gap you logged earlier. You keep your hand steady on the shutdown switch, aware that you have identified a safe transmission route but you do not press the key. The station hums around you, the future voice still echoing, waiting for a decision you have not yet made.

displayed_scene.text:
You stare at the digital clock flashing 23:40, the rain drumming a steady rhythm against the cracked window. The fixed receiver crackles, replaying your own exhausted voice—older, strained—begging you not to shut the line. Three low notes linger, then a breath fills the silence.

You pull the station log from the metal tray, the paper still warm from the lamp. With a steady hand, you compare the timestamp stamped on the recording with the clock on the wall. The tape reads 00:00, exactly twenty minutes ahead of the present time. Your pen scratches a line across the page: "Recording timestamp 00:00, station clock 23:40 – discrepancy noted. No transmission sent yet."

The recorder continues its loop, the notes echoing in the dim, salty air. Your hand hovers over the shutdown switch, the decision looming as the rain darkens the breakwater beyond the glass.
